# Isaiah 20: Research notes

**A note on coverage:** The two web tools ran out before I could reach bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any site discussing prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. I also found no page on Isaiah 20 from ligonier, desiringgod, gty, seedbed, the Lutheran sites or the Pentecostal journals. Those sections are left out. I found that Haydock's Catholic commentary covers this chapter, but I didn't read it. The "tradition" points below come from individual older commentators, not official church positions.

---

## v. 1: Ashdod falls to "the Tartan"

**What happened:**
- Ashdod was a Philistine city. Its fall would have made Judah think "We're next. We need protection." Guzik dates it to 711 B.C. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Utley also gives 711 B.C. He says the king of Ashdod rebelled in 713 and Sargon II's army put the revolt down in 711. He notes this verse is the only place the Old Testament names Sargon. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20
- Ellicott draws on Sargon's own records. Ashdod's king refused to pay tribute and was replaced. The people then chose a new king, and Sargon took the city and carried off its gods and treasure. This pushed Hezekiah's advisers to look to Egypt for protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm

**"Tartan":**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "Tartan" is a title, not a name. It means "commander-in-chief," the second-highest post in the empire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm
- Utley says the word means a field general. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

**The dating is debated:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Ashdod was besieged twice under Sargon, in 713 and 711. It thinks this verse means the first siege, led by the Tartan, because Sargon led the second one himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm
- A Broadman commentary, quoted by Coffman, dates the event to 711 from Sargon's inscriptions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-1.html

**Who was Sargon? (older vs. newer readings):**
- Several older writers thought "Sargon" was another name for Sennacherib. These include Barnes, Benson and Clarke, who cite Jerome's claim that Sennacherib had seven names. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-1.html
- Barnes admits that who Sargon was "is not certainly known." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm
- Gill lists several options: Shalmaneser, Sennacherib or Esarhaddon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-1.html

**Why the city mattered:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says Ashdod was the key to Egypt in that region, so taking it had to come before invading Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm

**Calvin's view:** Calvin says the chapter picks up chapter 19's warning about Egypt. It shows that Israel would be shamed by Egypt's punishment because they had trusted Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-1.html

*(None of the pages I read explains the BSB wording "Before the year." The NET Bible translates it as the message given "during the year.")* https://biblehub.com/parallel/isaiah/20-1.htm

## v. 2: Sackcloth and sandals off

**What was the sackcloth?**
- **Prophet's garment:** The Pulpit Commentary thinks it was the rough haircloth prophets usually wore (compare Elijah and John the Baptist). It mentions Dr. Kay's alternative view that Isaiah wore sackcloth only for a time of mourning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-2.htm
- **Mourning clothes:** Guzik calls it clothes of mourning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- **Sign of grief:** The Geneva notes say it showed Isaiah grieving over the coming disaster. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-2.htm
- **Either:** Utley notes sackcloth and bare feet normally meant mourning, but Isaiah may have been taking off the symbol of his prophetic office. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

**What did "naked" mean?** Most say it meant stripped to an undergarment, not fully nude:
- Guzik says Isaiah wore only the inner garment. The point was poverty and humiliation, "not nudity." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Benson and Poole say Isaiah went without his outer garment, as slaves and prisoners did. Poole points to 1 Samuel 19:24 and John 21:7 for this use of "naked." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-2.htm
- Utley says most uses of the Hebrew word mean partly clothed. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20
- Coffman, quoting Delitzsch, says the act went against custom, not against decency. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-20.html

**Why it was done:**
- Poole, quoted by Guzik, says God sometimes added a visible sign to his prophets' words to make people take the message seriously. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Calvin says the act would have been ridiculous if Isaiah had done it on his own. Because God commanded it, it should inspire awe. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-2.html

## v. 3: "My servant… three years… a sign and omen"

**What the sign meant:**
- Isaiah dressed as a defeated captive. The three-year sign warned Judah over a long period not to trust Egypt and Cush. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/20-3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes how rarely God calls someone "my servant": Abraham, Moses, Caleb, Job and a few others share the title. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
- Matthew Henry says God gave Isaiah this title because he obeyed in something others probably laughed at. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-3.html
- JFB says this is Isaiah's only strictly symbolic act. Such acts were common in later prophets like Jeremiah and Ezekiel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
- Ellicott thinks Isaiah acted in silence and explained the sign only when the three years ended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm

**The main debate: what do the "three years" refer to?**
- **He did it for three full years.**
  - Ellicott sees no good reason to shorten it to one day or three days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say Isaiah dressed this way whenever he appeared as a prophet for three whole years. It foretold Egypt-Ethiopia's fall at the end of that time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
  - Coffman criticizes commentators who contradict the text on this point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-20.html
  - Utley says Isaiah shocked his culture by going partly naked for three years. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20
- **Three years, but only at times.**
  - Poole and Benson: only when he went out among the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
  - Henry: whenever he appeared as a prophet. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-3.html
  - Wolf, quoted by Guzik: perhaps part of each day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- **"A three-year sign," meaning the years belong to the event, not the act.**
  - Barnes, followed by JFB, reads it as a sign of a three-year disaster for Egypt. He thinks three years of acting would not fit the urgent crisis, and mentions Lowth's guess of three days, with a day for each year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
  - Gill argues from the Hebrew accent marks that the years go with what the sign points to. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-3.html
  - Clarke agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-2.html
  - The Cambridge Bible, quoted on Bible Hub, calls this reading "very unnatural." It thinks the reading was driven by a wish to avoid a long-lasting act. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-2.htm
- **Only in a vision.** Calvin says the general view in his day was that it happened in a vision, once. He disagrees, pointing out the text adds "he did so." He thinks Isaiah went naked whenever he acted as a prophet, uncovering only what could be seen without shame. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-2.html

**Lessons drawn:** Bible Hub's study notes see God's patience in a long warning. They also read "three" as a symbol of completeness. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/20-3.htm

## v. 4: Captives led away naked

- Barnes stresses the word "so": as Isaiah was stripped, Egypt would be stripped of everything it had. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-4.htm
- Poole says "lead away" is the word used for driving animals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-4.htm
- Gill, and Wesley's Notes, compare the cut garments to how the Ammonites treated David's servants (2 Samuel 10:4). Gill says it was meant to humble Egypt's pride. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-4.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-20.html
- JFB, citing the explorer Belzoni, says Egyptian monuments show captives this way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-4.htm
- Utley reads the phrases as idioms. "Young and old" means the whole population, "naked" means shame (they still wore an undergarment) and "barefoot" means mourning. He links nakedness to the curse of exile in Deuteronomy 28:48. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

**When was it fulfilled? (views differ):**
- The Pulpit Commentary: about twelve years later, at Sennacherib's victory at Eltekeh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-1.htm
- A comment on StudyLight: Ashurbanipal's destruction of Thebes in 663. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-4.html
- Utley: several times, when parts of Egypt's army were captured and exiled. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

**Spiritual applications:**
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik, compares the scene to the devil driving sinners "hellward." They lack the white robe of Christ's righteousness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Thomas Coke, an early Methodist leader, draws a similar lesson about "slaves of sin." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/isaiah-20.html
- Coffman says the scene also hinted at Judah's own future fate, though that would come from Babylon, not Assyria. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/isaiah-20.html

## v. 5: "Dismayed and ashamed"

- Guzik: when we put our hope or pride in the wrong thing, God finds a way to make it fail us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Guzik, quoting Morgan: all hope not centred in God is "doomed to disappointment." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary: those who sought Egypt's help would be ashamed of their folly and afraid of what would follow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-20.html
- Matthew Henry: when our human props fail, that should drive us to God, not to despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
- Utley points out how often "dismayed" and "ashamed" appear in Isaiah. He says both are central to the book's message. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

## v. 6: "This coastland… How then can we escape?"

**Who are the people of "this coastland"? (views differ):**
- **Mainly Philistia.** Ellicott includes Philistia and Phoenicia, perhaps Cyprus too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
- **Palestine as a whole.**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes that Sargon described the rebel states as "dwelling beside the sea." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
  - Coke says it means all Palestine, not just Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/isaiah-20.html
- **Must include Judah.** The Cambridge Bible says Isaiah did not go about naked "for the sake of the Philistines." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
- **Chiefly Judah.**
  - Keil & Delitzsch hold this view, following Jerome, while including the rest of Palestine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
  - Gill says it is the land of Israel, following the Jewish commentators Rashi and Kimchi. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
  - Matthew Henry, the Geneva notes and Wesley's Notes say much the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-20.html

**The cry "How can we escape?":**
- Barnes: if the stronger nation fell, how could the weaker escape? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
- Poole adds that Hezekiah himself was largely free of this habit of trusting Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm
- Guzik: Judah was boxed in between two empires with no way out except the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-20/
- Calvin: those who refuse the refuge God offers will end up "naked and destitute." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-20.html
- Utley links the chapter to Isaiah's later warnings against an alliance with Egypt (chapters 30–31). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-20

**On how prophecy is fulfilled:** Keil & Delitzsch (older scholarship) say the fulfilment was real but did not match every expectation. Egypt was not converted and Assyria did not end. They conclude that the fulfilment is divine, but the prophecy itself is "both divine and human." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm

---

## Where commentators really disagree

1. **Whether Isaiah literally did it.** Calvin reports that most people in his day thought it was only a vision, and he rejects that. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/20-2.html
2. **What the three years refer to.** The options are three full years, three years at intervals, or "a three-year sign" with a shorter act. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-3.htm
   - The Methodist Wesley/Coke line takes "a three-year sign." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/isaiah-20.html
   - Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian) insists on three literal years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-20.html
3. **Who "this coastland" means.** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/20-6.htm

These splits run between individual commentators. They do not follow denominational lines.
